title: OpenAI employee charged after hidden recorder found in executive conference room
summary: What federal prosecutors allege about the hidden audio recorder found in an OpenAI executive conference room, the evidence described and the pending case.

# OpenAI employee charged after hidden recorder found in executive conference room


By OpenTools Team


·


October 13, 2026


Federal prosecutors allege an OpenAI engineer installed an encrypted audio recorder behind a television in a San Francisco executive conference room. The device was found September 30; the employee was arrested October 9 and remains presumed innocent.


##


Prosecutors allege a recorder was hidden behind a conference-room television


The[Justice Department said on October 13](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/saudi-national-arrested-installing-surreptitious-audio-recording-device-openai) that OpenAI personnel discovered an audio recording device on September 30 in an executive conference room in a San Francisco office. According to the criminal complaint described by prosecutors, the device was inserted into a USB port behind a television, concealed in toilet paper and installed around September 28. Its contents were encrypted.


Federal authorities charged OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He was arrested October 9 and made his first federal-court appearance October 13.


These are allegations in a pending criminal case. Alfozan is presumed innocent unless proven guilty, and the complaint is not a conviction or a finding that every alleged fact occurred.


##


The room handled technical, commercial and government discussions


The[DOJ release](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/saudi-national-arrested-installing-surreptitious-audio-recording-device-openai) says the conference room frequently hosted discussions involving proprietary research, product plans, business-development opportunities, government engagements and commercial relationships. That describes the sensitivity of the location; it does not establish what the device successfully captured.


Prosecutors did not publish the recordings, a duration of captured audio or a list of meetings recorded. The device's encrypted contents and the government's allegation that it could intercept conversations should therefore be kept separate from proof of what information left the room.


OpenAI later said it had no indication the employee improperly accessed or took model weights, source code or customer data, according to the[San Francisco Standard](https://sfstandard.com/2026/10/13/openai-engineer-arrested-alleged-bugging-executive-conference-room/) . That company statement does not resolve what audio, if any, was stored or transmitted.


##


The complaint describes CCTV, internal searches and device-specific chatbot prompts


Prosecutors say office CCTV showed Alfozan near the executive conference room on multiple dates even though he was not authorized to enter it or attend meetings there. The complaint also alleges he used a productivity tool to ask about OpenAI buildings, room capacities, calendars, leadership locations and outside-partner meetings.


The[DOJ account](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/saudi-national-arrested-installing-surreptitious-audio-recording-device-openai) further says a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse, sharing identifiers and attributes with his account, submitted prompts about building, hiding, remotely accessing and encrypting a continuous audio recorder. Prosecutors allege some prompts referenced the discovered device's custom header and unique MAC address.


The government did not allege in its press release that the spouse personally wrote those prompts. Account association, device identifiers and authorship are separate questions that the court process will have to test.


##


Security found a second similar device in an unattended bag


The complaint alleges that on October 5, CCTV captured Alfozan entering the conference room and looking behind the television. Prosecutors also say that OpenAI security opened an unattended bag in another room and found his wallet, identification and a second recording device similar to the first.


That second-device allegation matters because it is a separate physical item tied in the complaint to identifying property. It still does not by itself prove who installed the conference-room recorder, what it captured or why.


The publicly released evidence image shows the first device positioned behind the television and, separately, exposed hardware on a table. OpenTools has preserved the image without generative alteration; only a 16:9 crop and downscaling were applied for the hero.


##


The charge carries a possible five-year maximum, not a sentence


If convicted, Alfozan faces a statutory maximum of five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release, according to the[Justice Department](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/saudi-national-arrested-installing-surreptitious-audio-recording-device-openai) . Maximum penalties are not forecasts of a sentence.


The FBI is investigating, and prosecutors from the Northern District of California and the Justice Department's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section are handling the case. The[San Francisco Standard](https://sfstandard.com/2026/10/13/openai-engineer-arrested-alleged-bugging-executive-conference-room/) reports that a detention hearing is scheduled for October 19.


The next reliable milestones are the complaint and future court filings, a detention decision, any indictment, discovery tested by the defense and eventual disposition. Claims about espionage motive, foreign direction or stolen secrets should remain unproven unless prosecutors file evidence supporting them. Follow[OpenAI's OpenTools organization page](https://opentools.ai/organizations/openai) for material updates.
